articles.title: A revolutionary way of targeting tumours could beat even the worst cancers
articles.summary: We have long treated cancer based on its location in the body. But a whole new approach that analyses tumours differently is now helping people survive forms of cancer that were once considered a death sentence
articles.content:
We have long treated cancer based on its location in the body. But a whole new approach that analyses tumours differently is now helping people survive forms of cancer that were once considered a death sentence

Brian Stauffer

Stephen Huff was about to get married when he had a scan to investigate why he had been feeling short of breath. He was a fit 29-year-old who had played professional baseball and never smoked, so he wasn’t expecting the diagnosis: stage 4 lung cancer. “I had multiple spots all in my lungs, my neck, my spine, my liver, my brain – just everywhere,” he says. “I put on a brave front, but deep down I was terrified. I didn’t know if I’d be here in six months.”

Luckily for Huff, his mother, a cancer researcher, encouraged him to get a new kind of test that is quietly revolutionising treatment. Rather than focusing on the place in the body where the cancer originated – for example, the lungs, bowel or skin – the new approach focuses on genes. The aim is to pinpoint the exact mutation driving the tumour, so it can be switched off with targeted drugs that act like guided missiles.

Through this fresh approach, Huff “hit the lottery” – as his oncologist told him – because it meant he could be treated with a recently approved drug that specifically targeted the genetic alteration driving his cancer. Within weeks, Huff began to feel better. “My first scan showed that basically every tumour site had either shrunk or gone away completely,” he says.

Advertisement

Now, thanks to this precision oncology method, more and more people like Huff are surviving cancers that were once considered a death sentence, like lung, pancreatic and brain cancer. “Being able to identify exactly what makes a cancer tick is having an incredible impact,” says David Thomas, a pioneer of precision oncology at the University of New South Wales in Sydney. But surprisingly, it has received little fanfare outside of the medical community so far.

In the past, most cancer drugs were discovered by chance. The common chemotherapy drug cisplatin, for example, was stumbled upon by scientists playing around with platinum electrodes and bacteria in the 1960s. Paclitaxel, another widely used drug, was isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew tree and hit on during random screening of plant extracts. Both work by killing rapidly dividing cells, regardless of whether they are in a person’s cancer or elsewhere. This is like dropping a large bomb on the body, inflicting mass damage and causing side effects like fatigue, nausea and hair loss, but often still missing cancer cells hiding inside deep bunkers.

Over time, blind trial and error worked out which of these drugs worked best for each cancer type, based on its anatomical location and appearance under a microscope. The type of lung cancer that Huff had, for example, was non-small cell lung cancer, named for the large size of its cells when viewed under a microscope. Decades of trialling different drugs in this specific cancer type identified that a combination of cisplatin and paclitaxel seemed to treat it best. However, it still gave people an average of only eight months to live.

The new era of precision oncology is instead informed by the exact gene that has gone awry in a person’s cancer, rather than by its broad anatomical location or cellular appearance. “Cancer is fundamentally a genetic disease,” says Thomas. “So, by pinpointing the precise genes responsible for cancer, and rationally designing drugs to target those individual genes, we are making rapid strides.”

DNA sequencing is revolutionising cancer treatment by pinpointing the exact mutations driving a tumour Cavan Images/Alamy

The first seeds of precision oncology were planted in the 1990s and early 2000s, when scientists discovered a handful of genes that spurred cancer growth if they became mutated or mixed up. A gene called EGFR, for example, was shown to be relevant to the development of some lung cancers, and two others, BCR and ABL1, to chronic myeloid leukaemia, a blood cancer. These discoveries paved the way for some of the first targeted drugs, including one called imatinib, which blocks an abnormal cancer-promoting protein that is produced when the BCR and ABL1 genes mistakenly fuse together. Since imatinib was introduced in 2001, the survival rate for chronic myeloid leukaemia eight years after diagnosis has shot up to almost 90 per cent.

The field picked up momentum in the 2010s, when it became possible to rapidly sequence not just one gene in a cancer’s cells, or a small panel of genes, but hundreds in a single test. It became known as comprehensive genomic profiling, or comprehensive biomarker testing.

The test that Huff undertook, for instance, looked at over 300 genes in a biopsy of one of the tumours in his neck. It found that his cancer was being driven by an alteration in a gene called ALK that is involved in cell growth. Identifying the gene meant he could be treated with a drug called alectinib, which specifically targets this alteration.

Thomas oversaw one of the early trials of comprehensive genomic profiling, launched by the Garvan Institute of Medical Research in Sydney in 2016. It enrolled almost 4000 people with advanced cancers like lung, pancreatic, brain, ovarian, bowel and breast cancer who had exhausted all available treatment options. Samples of their tumours were collected by biopsy and sequenced to examine more than 500 cancer-relevant genes. Over a third of participants were found to have telltale changes in at least one gene that meant they could be recommended a targeted drug. They ended up living almost twice as long as those who weren’t matched to a treatment. “It was so successful we had patients flying over from Western Australia so they could take part,” says Thomas.

Researchers at Australia’s Zero Childhood Cancer project have the ambitious goal of stopping all childhood cancer deaths Children's Cancer Institute

Based on the trial’s success, the Australian government agreed to fund a nationwide programme, led by Thomas, which launched in 2023. It offers free comprehensive genomic profiling and tailored treatment recommendations to all Australians with cancers that have low survival prospects. So far, over 26,000 people have signed up.

The outlooks for these participants have become increasingly rosy. “Now, about 48.5 per cent are getting a strong recommendation, meaning we know with reasonable confidence that they will live longer if they receive the recommended treatment,” says Thomas.

Targeting the worst cancers

This is even the case for pancreatic cancer, known as the “worst of the worst” cancer, because it is often survived for only a few months. “We’ve found that over 30 per cent of patients with pancreatic cancer who receive a good treatment recommendation are alive past five years, compared to 4 per cent who don’t get a match,” says Thomas. This is mostly because the testing can identify individuals who are likely to respond to immunotherapy drugs called checkpoint inhibitors, which stop cancer cells from disarming the immune system.

Things are set to get even better, now that a drug called daraxonrasib has just been approved in the US. It targets mutations in a gene called KRAS that are commonly found in pancreatic cancer and, in the latest clinical trial, it doubled survival time for those with advanced forms of the cancer.

Another of the most feared malignancies is brain cancer, but precision oncology is starting to make inroads here, too. A new drug called vorasidenib targets mutations in genes called IDH1 and IDH2, which often trigger the growth of brain tumours called gliomas. In a clinical trial, people with gliomas caused by these mutations were 61 per cent less likely to experience worsening of their cancer during the study period if they received vorasidenib compared with a placebo.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

As the evidence stacks up, countries like Japan, Germany, Norway and Denmark have recently made comprehensive genomic profiling routinely available to all those with advanced cancers as part of their public healthcare systems.

The picture is more complicated in the UK. Most people with advanced cancers are now eligible for comprehensive genomic profiling through National Health Service (NHS) systems across the UK. But despite hundreds of genes being sequenced in each person’s tumour as part of a standard test, the results are reported for only around one to 10 genes based on the cancer type and whether treatments are available on the NHS. For example, ALK gene alterations are reported for lung cancer because alectinib is already available via the UK’s health system.

“This supports optimal treatment for standard care, but there’s untapped potential for identifying people who could be recruited into clinical trials for new treatments,” says Matthew Krebs, an oncologist and researcher at the University of Manchester, UK. To address this, he and his colleagues recently advocated for NHS England to add an extra 30 “research genes” to the small panel currently reported, with the hope of eventually increasing this number.

The US doesn’t have a nationally coordinated precision oncology programme, instead relying on a patchwork of services led by various universities and research institutes. “There’s quite a bit of competition in terms of different academic centres wanting to have programmes like this for their catchment areas,” says Jens Rueter, who runs the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative at the Jackson Laboratory, an independent research institute. But despite this, only a minority of people with advanced cancer in the US, about 1 in 4, undergo comprehensive genomic profiling. This has been put down to a lack of awareness and socioeconomic and geographic disparities in access.

Tumour-agnostic drugs

As well as improving access to testing, there is a need to improve access to the drugs that are then recommended by that testing. Sometimes, for example, an individual with ovarian cancer is recommended a drug that is currently approved only for breast cancer, meaning they can access it only if they pay for it out of pocket. To address this challenge, some drugs are now being approved as “tumour-agnostic drugs”, meaning that they can be prescribed for any cancer, regardless of where it is.

Another headache for precision oncology is the issue of drug resistance. The ability of new drugs to precisely hit their intended targets is both a strength and a weakness – it maximises efficacy and minimises side effects, but also means that, over time, a person’s cancer can devise workarounds. That means we have to keep building up our arsenal of targeted drugs.

In Huff’s case, alectinib worked for five years, but then his cancer started progressing again. Fortunately, by that time, a new ALK-targeted drug called lorlatinib had been approved. Again, his tumours shrank, and four years on, he says his health is great. He is now married with two children and works in medical technology sales. “Life is really good; I’m just trying to cherish it for as long as I can,” he says.

One of the brightest lights in the world of precision oncology is a programme called Zero Childhood Cancer, which is available to all children in Australia with cancer. It goes beyond what is offered in adult programmes in an effort to meet an ambitious goal of cutting childhood cancer deaths down to zero.

Eliminating childhood cancer

When a child is enrolled in the programme, the whole genome of their cancer is sequenced, not just a few hundred genes. Extra tests, called RNA whole transcriptome sequencing and methylation profiling, are performed on top of this to give an even clearer picture of what is driving their cancer. In addition, the genome that the child was born with in their normal cells is sequenced to try to identify why they developed cancer in the first place. Finally, in some cases, the child’s cancer cells are grown in a lab so that a robot can test over 100 different cancer drugs on them, or are grown in a mouse to test the potential efficacy of a specific drug.

Jack Kennelly is one of Zero’s success stories. He was diagnosed with a fast-growing brain tumour when he was 3 years old, after telling his parents that his head hurt. He was found to have a mutation in a gene called DICER1, which had triggered the growth of a rare form of cancer in his brain. DICER1 normally functions as a tumour-suppressor gene, but certain mutations stop it from working, leading to unchecked cell growth.

Jack Kennelly is one of the children who have benefited from the gene-focused approach to cancer treatment being pioneered in Australia The Kennelly family

No targeted drugs are yet available for DICER1-related cancers, but the finding meant that Jack could be given a combination of three chemotherapy drugs that had previously been shown to be most effective for treating his rare form of cancer. This regime, in combination with surgery and radiation, wiped out Jack’s brain tumour. “He went in and had an MRI, and they called us and said, ‘It’s gone’,” says his mother, Kristen. “Words can’t really express how incredible that feeling was.” Jack is now 7, and “just little things like school assemblies are different for us because he’s up there doing his thing, he is full of joy, and we’re so thankful every day that he is still with us”, says Kristen.

The finding that Jack carries a DICER1 mutation in the genome he was born with also means that his ongoing monitoring can be precisely tailored. Before the age of 8, DICER1 mutations are most likely to trigger tumour growth in the kidneys, so he currently gets regular scans of this area. “The next thing will be his thyroid,” says Kristen. The worry is endless, but the regular surveillance is designed to detect any new tumours while they are still at an early, treatable stage.

Louis Chesler, the director of Children’s Cancer Institute in Sydney, which coordinates the Zero programme, says he now believes “more than ever” that children dying from cancer will eventually become a thing of the past. “It’s not a matter of if, but when,” he says. “It’s the most empowering time I can ever think of to be a researcher or clinician in medicine.” Emerging technologies like personalised cancer vaccines, blood tests for early detection of cancer recurrences and AI-assisted drug discovery will make precision oncology even more powerful, he says.

For Thomas, precision oncology has become deeply personal. Four years ago, while he was busy setting up Australia’s nationwide programme, he himself was diagnosed with cancer and enrolled in his own programme. “Fortunately, I have a cancer that is responding to some of these brilliant treatments,” he says. “At this point, I don’t think I’m likely to be cured, but I am still able to make a meaningful contribution, both professionally and personally,” he adds. “I’m a poster child of what modern medicine can achieve.”

It highlights broad, meaningful impacts on many cancer types and includes detailed evidence of success, ongoing programs, and future potential, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news with substantial real-world benefits.
articles.personality_title: New gene-focused cancer treatment offers hope for tough cases
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Cancer has traditionally been treated based on where it starts in the body, like the lungs or pancreas. Treatments often used strong drugs that attacked many cells, causing serious side effects and limited success.

**What happened** – A new approach called precision oncology looks at the specific genetic changes causing a person’s cancer. By testing hundreds of genes in a tumor, doctors can find exact mutations and use special drugs that target those changes. For example, Stephen Huff, diagnosed with advanced lung cancer, was treated with a drug targeting a gene mutation, shrinking his tumors and extending his life.

**Impact** – This gene-based method is improving survival for many cancers once considered deadly, including lung, pancreatic, and brain cancers. In Australia, a program offers free gene testing and personalized treatments, helping nearly half of patients live longer. Childhood cancer treatments have also advanced by sequencing entire cancer genomes and testing many drugs to find the best fit.

**What's next step** – More countries are starting to offer this testing widely, and new drugs are being approved to target common mutations. Researchers are working to overcome drug resistance and expand access to treatments. Programs like Australia’s Zero Childhood Cancer aim to eliminate childhood cancer deaths by using these advanced methods.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By focusing on cancer’s genetic mutations instead of its location, precision oncology is changing treatment and helping patients live longer with cancers once seen as unstoppable.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le cancer était traditionnellement traité selon son emplacement dans le corps, comme les poumons ou le pancréas. Les traitements utilisaient souvent des médicaments puissants attaquant de nombreuses cellules, causant des effets secondaires importants et un succès limité.

Par exemple, Stephen Huff, atteint d’un cancer du poumon avancé, a reçu un médicament ciblant une mutation génétique, réduisant ses tumeurs et prolongeant sa vie.

**Impact** – Cette méthode basée sur les gènes améliore la survie pour plusieurs cancers autrefois mortels, comme ceux du poumon, du pancréas et du cerveau. articles.personality_title_es: Un nuevo tratamiento de cáncer centrado en los genes ofrece esperanza para casos difíciles
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El cáncer se ha tratado tradicionalmente según su ubicación en el cuerpo, como los pulmones o el páncreas. Los tratamientos solían usar medicamentos fuertes que atacaban muchas células, causando efectos secundarios graves y resultados limitados.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo enfoque llamado oncología de precisión analiza los cambios genéticos específicos que causan el cáncer de una persona. Al examinar cientos de genes en un tumor, los médicos pueden encontrar mutaciones exactas y usar medicamentos dirigidos. Por ejemplo, Stephen Huff, diagnosticado con cáncer avanzado de pulmón, recibió un medicamento que atacaba una mutación genética, reduciendo sus tumores y prolongando su vida.

**Impacto** – Este método basado en genes está mejorando la supervivencia en muchos cánceres antes considerados mortales, como los de pulmón, páncreas y cerebro. En Australia, un programa ofrece pruebas genéticas gratuitas y tratamientos personalizados, ayudando a casi la mitad de los pacientes a vivir más tiempo. Los tratamientos para el cáncer infantil también han avanzado gracias a la secuenciación completa del genoma tumoral y la prueba de muchos medicamentos.

**Próximo paso** – Más países están comenzando a ofrecer estas pruebas de forma amplia, y se están aprobando nuevos medicamentos para mutaciones comunes. Los investigadores trabajan para superar la resistencia a los medicamentos y ampliar el acceso a los tratamientos. Programas como Zero Childhood Cancer en Australia buscan eliminar las muertes por cáncer infantil usando estos métodos avanzados.

**Resumen en una frase** – Al enfocarse en las mutaciones genéticas del cáncer en lugar de su ubicación, la oncología de precisión está cambiando el tratamiento y ayudando a los pacientes a vivir más tiempo con cánceres antes considerados incurables.

articles.title: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
articles.summary: A promising new treatment for knee arthritis uses tiny, dissolvable particles to block abnormal blood vessels, easing inflammation and pain without joint replacement surgery. In a study of 194 patients, 80% experienced clinically meaningful pain relief lasting at least 12 months.
articles.content:
A minimally invasive procedure that targets abnormal blood vessels in the knee could provide lasting relief for people struggling with osteoarthritis, offering a potential alternative to joint replacement surgery.

In a study involving 194 patients, researchers found that a treatment using tiny particles that dissolve within hours was associated with substantial reductions in knee pain and improvements in mobility. The benefits persisted for at least 12 months, with 80% of patients assessed at the one-year follow-up reporting clinically meaningful pain relief.

The approach, known as genicular artery embolization, aims to interrupt the inflammation and abnormal blood vessel growth that contribute to chronic knee pain. Rather than replacing the damaged joint, doctors use a thin catheter to deliver microscopic particles directly into specific blood vessels.

The findings, published in the journal Radiology, suggest that this technique could provide another option for patients who have exhausted conventional treatments but cannot or do not want to undergo knee replacement surgery.

Why Knee Arthritis Is So Difficult To Treat

Osteoarthritis is the world's most common form of arthritis and a major cause of disability. According to the World Health Organization, knee osteoarthritis affects more than 365 million adults worldwide.

The condition develops as cartilage, the protective tissue that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorates. But osteoarthritis involves more than cartilage damage. Inflammation within the joint, changes in surrounding tissues, and increased sensitivity of pain signaling nerves can all contribute to persistent discomfort.

For many people, the consequences extend far beyond occasional knee pain. Everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs, exercising, or standing for extended periods can become increasingly difficult.

Treatments typically begin with physical therapy, medication, and injections into the affected joint. When these approaches stop providing adequate relief, knee replacement surgery may eventually be considered. However, surgery is not appropriate or desirable for everyone.

"For many patients with knee osteoarthritis, there is a real treatment gap today," said Florian Nima Fleckenstein, M.D., deputy head of Interventional Radiology Campus Mitte, Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin. "Conservative measures such as intra-articular injections no longer provide sufficient relief, but joint replacement is not an option for medical or personal reasons."

A Different Way To Fight Knee Arthritis Pain

The treatment being investigated, genicular artery embolization (GAE), approaches knee arthritis from an unusual direction. Instead of focusing directly on damaged cartilage, it targets the abnormal blood vessels that develop around an inflamed joint.

These vessels can form within and around the synovium, a thin membrane lining the inside of the joint. As the vessels multiply, they can contribute to inflammation and encourage the growth of sensory nerves involved in transmitting pain.

GAE is designed to interrupt this process by reducing blood flow through the abnormal vessels while preserving the knee's normal circulation.

During the procedure, an interventional radiologist inserts a thin catheter into an artery and carefully guides it toward the affected blood vessels. Tiny particles are then injected to block selected vessels, with the goal of reducing inflammation and pain.

The technique is called superselective embolization because doctors target specific small arteries rather than blocking circulation throughout the joint. It does not require an open surgical incision or replacement of the knee.

Researchers have previously investigated both temporary blocking agents and permanent microscopic particles. Each approach has potential drawbacks, including differences in how precisely the particles can be delivered and how long they remain inside the blood vessels.

For this study, the team examined rapidly resorbable, gelatin-based microspheres. These precisely sized, spherical particles are engineered to dissolve within hours, potentially combining the advantages of temporary agents with the controlled delivery of permanent microspheres.

"GAE is a whole new treatment regimen that targets abnormal hypervascularity around the joint and, in turn, modulates the pathological neurovascular environment," Dr. Fleckenstein said.

Hypervascularity refers to an unusually high concentration of blood vessels. The pathological neurovascular environment describes the abnormal interactions between those vessels and pain signaling nerves in the affected tissue.

"By reducing both inflammation and pain, GAE with resorbable microspheres may be the first procedure that alters the course of the disease, slowing its progression."

Whether the procedure can actually slow osteoarthritis progression remains an open question. Although reducing inflammation could theoretically influence the disease, the study did not demonstrate that GAE prevents cartilage deterioration or reverses existing joint damage.

Nearly 200 Patients Underwent the Procedure

To evaluate the approach, researchers conducted a prospective single-center study involving 194 patients with osteoarthritis-related knee pain. The participants included 114 women and 80 men, with a median age of 69 years and a median body mass index of 28.4.

All had continued to experience symptoms despite at least three months of conventional care, including physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, and injections into the knee.

"We believe these results carry real weight because they come from real-world data," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "With this broad, inclusive study design, our participants are exactly the patients that physicians encounter every day in their practices."

The procedures took place between July and November 2024. Forty-five participants (23%) had osteoarthritis affecting both knees and received two separate treatments, with the second performed within four weeks of the first.

Altogether, the researchers carried out 239 GAE procedures.

Doctors used real-time X-ray imaging, known as fluoroscopy, to guide the catheter and deliver the particles to the targeted arteries. All 239 procedures were technically successful, meaning the intended blood vessels were successfully treated.

The safety findings were also encouraging. No moderate or severe adverse events were recorded, and mild, temporary complications occurred in 6.7% of procedures.

These included brief skin discoloration near the treated area and one superficial collection of blood near the catheter insertion site. All resolved without lasting complications.

Knee Arthritis Pain Dropped and Stayed Lower for a Year

The researchers monitored pain, movement, and quality of life before treatment and at several intervals afterward. Assessments were conducted at six weeks, three months, six months, and 12 months. An orthopedic surgeon also examined patients in person at the six-month follow-up.

Participant retention remained relatively high throughout the study. Follow-up rates were 94% at six weeks (183/194), 89% at three months (172/194), 89% at six months (171/194), and 79% at 12 months (154/194).

The most striking finding was the sustained reduction in knee pain.

Using the Numeric Rating Scale (a 0-to-10 measure of pain intensity), median pain scores fell from 7 before treatment to 4 after six weeks. By six months, the median score had declined to 3, and it remained at that level at the 12-month follow-up.

That represents a reduction of more than half from the original median pain score, with benefits that were still apparent a full year after treatment.

"In our cohort, we saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function, including sports and recreation and daily activity," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "Most importantly, their quality of life significantly increased."

Patients Also Reported Better Mobility and Quality of Life

The improvements extended beyond pain reduction. Researchers used the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, a standardized questionnaire that evaluates how knee problems affect symptoms, mobility, recreation, and everyday life.

Across all five areas assessed, patients reported meaningful progress during the year following treatment.

Median scores for daily activities increased from 53 to 71.5, suggesting that routine movements such as walking and climbing stairs became easier. Sports and recreation scores climbed from 15 to 36, indicating improvements in more physically demanding activities.

Scores measuring osteoarthritis symptoms rose from 51 to 68, while the pain category improved from 44 to 65 (where 0 indicates extreme knee pain and 100 indicates no pain at all).

Quality of life scores also increased substantially, rising from 19 before treatment to 40 after 12 months.

To determine whether these changes were large enough to matter to patients, the researchers applied established thresholds for clinically meaningful improvement.

Previous studies have identified a reduction of at least 2.0 points on the Numeric Rating Scale and an increase of at least 10 points in the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score categories as meaningful improvements.

These thresholds are known as the minimum clinically important difference. In simple terms, they distinguish changes that are likely to be noticeable in daily life from smaller statistical differences that may have little practical significance.

At 12 months, 80% of participants who completed the pain assessment exceeded the clinically meaningful improvement threshold.

"Our study demonstrates that GAE using rapidly resorbable gelatin-based microspheres is a safe, minimally invasive therapy that provides meaningful pain relief and functional improvement in participants with osteoarthritis-related knee symptoms for at least 12 months," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "By embolizing the pathological vessels, we're able to normalize the vessel structure -- and, in turn, the neuronal structure of the knee."

What Other Studies Reveal About Knee Artery Embolization

The results add to a growing body of evidence investigating whether blocking abnormal knee blood vessels can offer sustained relief from osteoarthritis.

A randomized study published in Clinical Radiology in 2026 provided encouraging findings. Researchers compared GAE combined with standard care against standard care alone in 50 patients. After one year, pain scores had improved by 72.7% in the embolization group, compared with 24.2% in the standard care group. The treated patients also reported better knee function.

However, that study used polyvinyl alcohol particles rather than the dissolving gelatin particles examined by Fleckenstein's team. It also did not include a sham procedure, making it difficult to separate the treatment's physical effects from patients' expectations.

Other research has raised important questions about how much of the improvement is caused by embolization itself.

A randomized, sham-controlled study published in European Radiology in April 2026 followed 58 patients for 12 months. Both the GAE and sham treatment groups experienced sustained reductions in pain, but researchers found no statistically significant difference between them. MRI examinations also failed to identify a significant reduction in joint inflammation attributable to embolization.

Similarly, an analysis appearing in the September 2026 issue of the European Journal of Radiology examined 22 studies involving 633 patients. Although pain scores often improved substantially after treatment, the researchers found no statistically significant advantage over sham procedures when results from three randomized trials were combined.

A separate June 2026 analysis of 45 studies involving 2,205 patients also documented improvements in pain and function, but judged the overall certainty of the evidence to be low or very low.

Together, these findings suggest that GAE is associated with promising improvements, particularly in observational studies, but more rigorous trials are needed to establish how much benefit comes directly from blocking the blood vessels.

Could This Treatment Help Patients Avoid Knee Replacement?

Despite the remaining uncertainties, researchers and medical specialists are increasingly exploring GAE as a possible option for patients who have limited alternatives.

In a 2026 position statement, the Society of Interventional Radiology supported offering the procedure to appropriately selected patients whose symptoms persist despite conservative treatment, particularly those who cannot undergo or wish to delay knee replacement surgery.

The society also emphasized the importance of specialist training, careful patient selection, and continued clinical trials to establish the treatment's effectiveness and long-term safety.

The study led by Fleckenstein provides particularly valuable information about rapidly resorbable gelatin microspheres. With nearly 200 participants, it represented the largest published clinical investigation of this specific approach at the time.

Still, because the study did not include an untreated or sham treatment comparison group, it cannot establish how much of the observed improvement resulted directly from the procedure. The researchers also did not evaluate whether the treatment slows cartilage loss or prevents patients from eventually needing joint replacement.

Longer follow-up and larger controlled trials will be essential to determine how durable the benefits are, which patients respond best, and whether dissolving particles offer advantages over other embolization materials.

For patients whose knee arthritis continues to interfere with everyday life despite medication, therapy, and injections, the approach nevertheless represents an increasingly studied possibility.

"This lets us speak about safety and efficacy with real confidence," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "For the right patient, it can mean lasting relief from a single, minimally invasive procedure -- a meaningful new option between injections and joint replacement."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a promising new minimally invasive treatment for knee osteoarthritis that provides lasting pain relief and improved mobility for a large patient group, potentially offering a significant alternative to joint replacement surgery. The study involved nearly 200 patients and demonstrated substantial, clinically meaningful benefits lasting at least 12 months, addressing a major global health issue with broad impact and detailed context.
articles.personality_title: New minimally invasive treatment eases knee arthritis pain for a year
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Knee osteoarthritis is a common condition where the protective cartilage in the knee wears down, causing pain and difficulty moving. Many people try physical therapy, medicine, and injections, but if these don’t work, surgery to replace the knee is often the last option. However, surgery is not suitable or wanted by everyone.

**What happened** – Researchers tested a new treatment called genicular artery embolization (GAE) on 194 patients with knee arthritis. This treatment uses tiny, dissolvable particles injected through a thin tube to block abnormal blood vessels in the knee that cause inflammation and pain. The procedure is done without surgery. After treatment, 80% of patients reported meaningful pain relief that lasted at least 12 months, along with better movement and quality of life.

**Impact** – This treatment is different because it targets the blood vessels causing inflammation rather than the damaged cartilage itself. It is minimally invasive, has a low risk of side effects, and can help people who do not want or cannot have knee replacement surgery. The results show pain dropped by more than half and daily activities became easier for many patients.

**What's next step** – More studies with control groups are needed to confirm how much of the improvement is directly due to the treatment and to see if it can slow down arthritis over time. Doctors will also explore which patients benefit the most and how this method compares to others. For now, it offers a promising option between injections and surgery.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new, non-surgical treatment using tiny dissolvable particles can significantly reduce knee arthritis pain and improve movement for at least a year in many patients.

articles.title: Scientists just gave the powerhouses of our cells a high-tech upgrade
articles.summary: Scientists have created a new coating for mitochondria that preserves their ability to produce energy, potentially opening the door to new treatments for diseases involving these tiny cellular powerhouses. The technology could one day help transfer healthy mitochondria into damaged cells, although its effectiveness in transplantation remains unproven.
articles.content:
Scientists have developed a way to coat mitochondria, the tiny structures that produce energy inside our cells, with advanced materials without interfering with their function. The achievement could eventually help researchers develop new approaches to treating diseases caused by malfunctioning mitochondria.

The research was conducted by IRCCS Fondazione Istituto Neurologico Carlo Besta (FINCB) and Politecnico di Milano through their joint BraiNs laboratory, established in 2023. The collaboration combines the mitochondrial biology expertise of Dr. Valeria Tiranti (FINCB), a researcher in the Medical Genetics and Neurogenetics Complex Unit (SC) and head of the Fondazione Mariani Centre for Paediatric Mitochondrial Diseases, with the chemistry and materials engineering expertise of Professor Pierangelo Metrangolo (Politecnico di Milano).

The findings were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS).

A New Way to Coat the Powerhouses of Our Cells

Mitochondria generate the energy that cells need to carry out their essential activities. When these structures malfunction, they can contribute to several diseases, many of them rare. Mitochondrial diseases are particularly harmful to organs and tissues that require large amounts of energy, including the brain and muscles. Effective treatment options for these conditions remain limited.

To explore new possibilities, the researchers turned to Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOF), a class of advanced materials whose properties can be tailored for different applications. The importance of these materials was highlighted by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar Yaghi for their work in this field.

Applying these materials to mitochondria presents a major challenge because the structures are extremely delicate and can easily lose their ability to function properly.

The research team overcame this obstacle by developing a technique that applies tiny amounts of MOF material directly to the mitochondrial surface. Crucially, tests showed that the coated mitochondria continued producing energy, demonstrating that the process could modify their surfaces without compromising this essential function.

Potential for Future Mitochondrial Treatments

One of the most promising aspects of the discovery is the ability to customize the coating for different purposes.

"The possibility of modifying the coating now opens up new research prospects: in the future, it will be possible to develop MOF with different characteristics depending on the objective, creating coatings capable of performing specific functions," observes Prof. Metrangolo.

A potential application is mitochondrial transplantation, an experimental technique intended to introduce healthy mitochondria into cells whose existing mitochondria are not functioning correctly. Researchers believe that specially engineered coatings might eventually make it easier to deliver healthy mitochondria and help them interact with the cells receiving them.

"A specifically designed coating could, in the future, facilitate this transfer and the interaction between mitochondria and cells," emphasizes Dr. Tiranti.

However, this possibility remains unproven. Additional research will be necessary to establish whether coated mitochondria perform better during transplantation than mitochondria without a coating.

The study was completed as part of a research project led by PhD candidate Marco D'Amato. Funding was provided through the "CALabria HUB per Ricerca Innovativa ed Avanzata (Cal.Hub.Ria)" project, supported under the Ministry of Health's Health Operational Plan (Piano Operativo Salute, POS).
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in coating mitochondria with advanced materials that preserve their energy-producing function, potentially enabling new treatments for mitochondrial diseases. This has broad implications for health, especially for diseases affecting vital organs, and represents a meaningful advancement with detailed context and potential future applications.

articles.title: Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03252-3Compounds inspired by the blockbuster weight-loss drugs are also being trialled for schizophrenia and Parkinson’s disease, among other conditions.
articles.content:
Heavy alcohol use can cause atrophy (shown in red) in parts of the brain. Credit: Medical Body Scans/Science Photo Library

The quest for GLP-1 drugs that can treat brain disorders is getting a fresh infusion of energy and funding. Pharmaceutical companies have plunged into developing GLP-1-related compounds to treat addiction, schizophrenia, depression and other conditions — building on years of work by academic scientists.

Last month, pharma giant Eli Lilly presented the first clinical results of brenipatide, a compound related to the company’s blockbuster obesity drug tirzepatide, for treatment of alcohol use disorder. Last week, biotechnology firm Kariya Pharmaceuticals shared early clinical results of a similar compound called KP405 for Parkinson’s disease. And biotechnology company Baseline Therapeutics plans to start a clinical trial in early 2027 of a GLP-1 compound for alcohol use disorder.

Why do obesity drugs seem to treat so many other ailments?

Researchers have long been interested in GLP-1 drugs’ potential against brain conditions. But, until recently, the pharmaceutical industry has not shared that interest, says Lorenzo Leggio, an addiction scientist at the National Institutes of Health in Baltimore, Maryland.

The companies’ new focus on these therapies could accelerate access for people who could benefit from them, says Christian Hendershot, an addiction scientist at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles.

“With the industry trials coming online, we’ll see this area of work grow even more quickly in the next couple of years,” Hendershot says. “Hopefully that will lead to one or more FDA approvals for GLP-1 therapies for addiction.”

Treating the brain

Some of the blockbuster obesity drugs, such as semaglutide, mimic the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). Others, such as tirzepatide, mimic both GLP-1 and the gut hormone gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP). Both hormones are involved in regulating blood-sugar levels, among other functions.

People taking GLP-1 receptor agonists commonly report a lack of interest in drinking alcohol and smoking, an unexpected effect that piqued the interest of addiction researchers. In 2025, Hendershot published the results1 of the first clinical trial of semaglutide in people with alcohol use disorder. The study found that semaglutide reduced the craving for alcohol and episodes of heavy drinking over time. It also lowered the amount of alcohol that participants consumed in a laboratory test.

Since then, two other clinical studies led by academics have found similar results2,3. The studies so far consistently show benefits that seem to be greater than those of the drugs that are currently approved for alcohol use disorder, says Hendershot.

Long half-life

Such results have encouraged pharmaceutical companies to pursue variations of GLP-1 drugs for substance-abuse disorders. One example is brenipatide, the GLP-1 and GIP mimic that Eli Lilly in Indianapolis, Indiana, has been testing for the treatment of alcohol use disorder. The drug remains active in the human body for longer than do approved GLP-1 drugs. According to data presented last month at the Psych Congress in New Orleans, Louisiana, its half-life is 9–12 days, as opposed to 5–7 days for other approved GLP-1 medications. The longer duration makes the drug especially suitable for people living with substance use disorders or psychiatric conditions, says Robert Nicholson, who leads medical affairs for psychiatry and substance use disorders at Eli Lilly.

Could the gut give rise to alcohol addiction?

But, other than the longer half-life, it’s not clear that there are major differences between this compound and the drugs now on the market, says Randy Seeley, an obesity specialist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

Beyond alcohol use disorder, brenipatide is in clinical trials for a wide range of brain-related conditions, including tobacco and opioid use disorder, depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

Another GLP-1 mimic aimed at alcohol use disorder is BT-001, which is being developed by Baseline Therapeutics in San Francisco, California. The company plans to start phase III trials of BT-001 in early 2027.

This represents a significant breakthrough with broad potential health benefits for many people suffering from these conditions. The article provides detailed context about ongoing trials, mechanisms, and the potential impact on treatment options, fulfilling criteria for inspiring and substantive good news.
